question: Is Ecuador legitimately in an 'internal armed conflict,' or is the label a pretext for expanded military powers?

sideA.label: Government Position
sideA.text: President Noboa and successive Interior Ministers argue that the scale, coordination, and armament of groups like Los Choneros and Los Lobos meet the threshold of a non-international armed conflict under international humanitarian law, justifying military combat operations, curfews, and suspension of certain rights under repeated states of emergency.

sideB.label: Rights Groups & Constitutional Court
sideB.text: Human Rights Watch and Ecuador's own Constitutional Court have questioned the legal basis for the 'internal armed conflict' designation, warning it has been used to loosen use-of-force rules and due-process protections, contributing to a documented rise in extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, and arbitrary detention.

resolution: The designation remains in effect as of August 2026, renewed through successive decrees; the Constitutional Court has not struck it down but has repeatedly flagged human rights concerns, and UN bodies have opened formal complaint tracking on enforced disappearances tied to security operations.

question: What was Ecuador's true 2024 homicide rate — did it fall or rise from 2023?

sideA.label: Decline Narrative
sideA.text: Some official and international datasets, citing a 14% year-on-year drop, place the 2024 rate at approximately 39.3 per 100,000, framing early 2024 militarization as an initial success before violence resurged.

sideB.label: Continued-Rise Narrative
sideB.text: Other trackers (Statista, Macrotrends) report a 2024 rate as high as 46.5 per 100,000 — an eightfold increase since 2018 — arguing the 'decline' framing reflects data lags and undercounting of gang-attributed and prison deaths rather than genuine improvement.

resolution: Regardless of methodology, all sources agree 2025 set a new record at 50.9 per 100,000, undercutting any 2024 'improvement' narrative and confirming Ecuador as Latin America's homicide-rate leader for a third straight year.

question: Were the four boys killed in the Las Malvinas case innocent civilians or gang-affiliated targets?

sideA.label: Family & Prosecution Account
sideA.text: Families and prosecutors established the boys — aged 11 to 15 — were unarmed, had just finished playing soccer, and had no established gang affiliation; the abduction and killing were characterized in court as torture and extrajudicial execution by soldiers operating in a militarized zone.

sideB.label: Initial Military Framing
sideB.text: In the immediate aftermath, military and some government officials suggested the boys were suspected of gang involvement or petty theft, framing the incident as connected to security operations rather than an unprovoked abduction.

resolution: An Ecuadorian court sentenced 11 of 17 soldiers to the maximum 34 years in December 2025, formally establishing the boys' innocence and the soldiers' culpability for abduction, torture, and killing — a landmark, if rare, accountability verdict.

question: Did the Noboa family's banana export business knowingly facilitate cocaine trafficking?

sideA.label: Investigative Reporting (OCCRP/MercoPress)
sideA.text: Leaked Ecuadorian police intelligence documents and intercepted Balkan trafficker communications show traffickers bragging about 'exclusive rights' to smuggle cocaine in Noboa Trading banana containers, with over half a ton (an estimated €26 million worth) seized between 2020 and 2022 despite flagrante delicto interceptions.

sideB.label: Noboa Family Response
sideB.text: The Noboa family and campaign characterize the shipments as unwitting exploitation of legitimate export logistics by criminal networks — a vulnerability shared by virtually all major container exporters — and note no criminal charges have been filed against family members.

resolution: As of mid-2026, no member of the Noboa family has been charged; the underlying seizure cases remain without prosecuted defendants despite in-country evidence, and the matter continues to surface as a recurring opposition talking point without judicial resolution.

question: Does deepening US security cooperation strengthen Ecuador's fight against trafficking, or erode its sovereignty?

sideA.label: Government & US Position
sideA.text: The Noboa administration and US State/Defense officials frame the SOFA-based troop rotations, FTO designations, and joint operations begun March 2026 as essential force multipliers against cartels too powerful for Ecuador's security forces to counter alone.

sideB.label: Sovereignty & Rights Critics
sideB.text: Opposition figures and rights groups point to the November 2025 referendum, where roughly 61% of voters rejected reopening foreign military bases, arguing that SOFA-based deployments circumvent the electorate's clearly stated rejection of a larger US military footprint — echoing the controversial 2000-2009 Manta Forward Operating Location.

resolution: US personnel continue operating in Ecuador under the SOFA framework rather than a fixed base, a distinction the government argues respects the referendum result; critics maintain the practical effect — sustained US military presence and joint operations — is what voters intended to reject.

question: Are the rising complaints of extrajudicial force a necessary cost of fighting narco-terrorism, or systematic abuse?

sideA.label: Security Establishment View
sideA.text: Officials argue that combat operations against heavily armed, terrorist-designated groups inherently produce contested use-of-force incidents, and that isolated abuses — like Las Malvinas — are being prosecuted, showing the system is self-correcting.

sideB.label: Human Rights Watch / UN View
sideB.text: HRW's July 2026 'A Dangerous Partnership' report and 51 UN-logged enforced disappearance complaints (2024-2025) argue the abuses are patterned rather than isolated, citing torture, arbitrary detention, and unexplained drone strikes on fishing boats during joint US-Ecuador operations.

resolution: Complaints of excessive force remained elevated in 2025 (249, down from 293 in 2024 but still the second-highest in a decade), and HRW has called for increased US congressional oversight — a request not yet acted upon as of August 2026.

question: Do Ecuador's repeated states of emergency reduce violence, or have they become a routinized political tool?

sideA.label: Government Justification
sideA.text: The government presents each new state of emergency — at least five declared since January 2024, most recently June 2026 — as a targeted, temporary response to specific homicide spikes, citing enhanced patrol authority and curfews as necessary tools.

sideB.label: Critics' View
sideB.text: Opposition figures and analysts note states of emergency have been declared around politically sensitive moments — including immediately before the April 2025 election — arguing the tool has become normalized as a governance default rather than an exceptional measure, with limited demonstrated effect on the underlying homicide trend.

resolution: Homicide rates rose through 2025 to a record high despite near-continuous states of emergency since January 2024, suggesting the measure alone has not reversed the violence trend, though the government maintains it prevents even higher tolls.

question: Does designating Los Choneros and Los Lobos as terrorist organizations appropriately target the threat, or inflate a criminal problem into a war footing?

sideA.label: Designation Proponents
sideA.text: Ecuadorian and US officials argue the groups' coordinated attacks on state institutions, targeting of judges and journalists, and links to the Sinaloa Cartel and CJNG meet the legal and practical definition of terrorism, unlocking military and financial tools (FTO sanctions, SDGT asset freezes) unavailable against ordinary organized crime.

sideB.label: Skeptics
sideB.text: Some legal scholars and rights groups warn that a 'terrorism' framework blurs the line between counter-narcotics policing and counter-insurgency warfare, lowering evidentiary and due-process standards and enabling the kind of military abuses documented in the Las Malvinas and HRW cases.

resolution: Both the domestic (2024) and US (September 2025) designations remain in force as of August 2026; violence has continued to rise since their adoption, leaving the framework's practical effectiveness — as distinct from its legal and diplomatic utility — contested.

question: Did the November 2025 referendum actually block an expanded US military presence?

sideA.label: Government Interpretation
sideA.text: The Noboa government maintains it has respected the referendum outcome, noting no permanent US base has been established and that all deployments — Manta Air Force personnel, SOFA-based rotations — operate under pre-existing bilateral agreements rather than the rejected constitutional amendment.

sideB.label: Opposition Interpretation
sideB.text: Critics argue the March 2026 joint operations and continued rotations of US personnel through Manta represent precisely the expanded foreign military presence voters rejected by a nearly two-to-one margin, regardless of the legal instrument used to authorize it.

resolution: No formal base agreement has been signed as of August 2026, but US operational presence in Ecuador has visibly expanded since the referendum, leaving the practical distinction between 'SOFA cooperation' and 'foreign base' a live political dispute.

question: Why has the Ecuadorian government not formally recognized the scale of internal displacement from gang violence?

sideA.label: NGO / Researcher Position
sideA.text: Organizations tracking displacement put the number of people internally displaced by criminal violence since 2021 at roughly 132,000, with more than 400,000 having left the country entirely — figures they say the government has been slow to formally acknowledge or address with dedicated policy.

sideB.label: Government Position
sideB.text: Ecuadorian authorities have not published an official comprehensive internal displacement count tied to criminal violence, treating most relocation as informal population movement rather than displacement requiring a distinct humanitarian response, distinguishing it from disaster- or conflict-driven displacement frameworks used elsewhere.

resolution: As of 2026, Ecuador still lacks a dedicated government stance or registry on gang-violence displacement, leaving NGO and academic estimates as the primary public data source on the issue.

question: Has the government genuinely retaken control of Ecuador's prisons, or do gangs still functionally run them?

sideA.label: Government Position
sideA.text: SNAI and the Noboa administration point to the new maximum-security mega-prisons (La Roca, El Encuentro) and the transfer of high-value inmates like Fito to isolated facilities as evidence that gang command-and-control from behind bars has been substantially disrupted.

sideB.label: Independent Assessment
sideB.text: InSight Crime and other analysts note that riots continued at a similar or higher tempo through 2025 — the Machala and Esmeraldas riots occurred within the same week in September 2025 — even after mega-prison construction began, suggesting gangs retain effective operational control within, and communication out of, the prison system.

resolution: Prison violence has continued at a high rate through 2025-2026 even as new maximum-security capacity has come online, indicating the government's stated goal of breaking gang control over prisons remains unmet as of mid-2026.

question: Are threats against Ecuadorian journalists driven mainly by criminal groups, or does the state security apparatus also contribute to a chilling effect?

sideA.label: Criminal-Source Framing
sideA.text: Most documented physical attacks and killings of journalists, such as Patricio Aguilar's March 2025 murder, are directly attributed to organized crime retaliation for reporting on gang activity and trafficking routes.

sideB.label: RSF Assessment
sideB.text: Reporters Without Borders has explicitly criticized Ecuadorian authorities' 'willingness to restrict, not protect' the press, pointing to a documented spike in death threats — four cases logged January-February 2026 alone, versus three for all of 2025 — that it says reflects an environment where state actors are seen as unwilling or unable to provide protection, compounding the criminal threat.

resolution: RSF and Fundamedios continue to document both criminal-group attacks and state inaction as contributing factors, with 22 aggressions by criminal/terrorist organizations against media recorded January-August 2025 alone and no comprehensive state journalist-protection program yet in place.

question: How much of Ecuador's tourism collapse is attributable to the security crisis versus other factors?

sideA.label: Security-Driven Explanation
sideA.text: Industry analysts directly link the 12.6% drop in 2024 arrivals, and the 43.4% decline from 2019 levels, to the surge in homicides — from 3 to 22 daily on average over five years — and international travel advisories issued after the January 2024 crisis and subsequent bombings.

sideB.label: Multi-Factor Explanation
sideB.text: Other analysts note Ecuador's tourism sector was already struggling from prolonged post-pandemic recovery, periodic nationwide power outages during the 2023-2024 energy crisis, and broader Latin American travel pattern shifts, arguing security is a major but not sole driver of the decline.

resolution: Government and industry data through 2024-2025 show the steepest declines concentrated in provinces under active states of emergency, lending weight to the security-driven explanation, though the energy crisis compounded the effect in the same period.

question: Was the assassination plot against Interior Minister John Reimberg a credible, imminent threat or a lower-level gang boast?

sideA.label: Government Account
sideA.text: Minister Reimberg and Ecuadorian intelligence describe a documented plot led by alias 'Willy,' first head of Los Tiguerones, to be carried out through captured lieutenant alias 'Gato Negro,' serious enough to warrant a presidential decree assigning Reimberg and his family full-time military and police protection.

sideB.label: Skeptical Reading
sideB.text: Some observers note high-profile threats against Ecuadorian officials are common amid the conflict and that formal protection decrees have at times been read as much as political signaling of resolve against gangs as strictly operational necessity.

resolution: 'Gato Negro' (Galo Javier Suárez Román) was captured in Colombia, extradited, and imprisoned at El Encuentro; Executive Decree 450 formalizing Reimberg's protection was issued in July 2026 and remains in effect, treating the threat as credible.

question: Did Adolfo 'Fito' Macías genuinely agree to extradition, or was it a negotiated outcome under duress?

sideA.label: Official Account
sideA.text: Ecuadorian and US authorities describe Macías as having formally accepted extradition following his June 2025 recapture, with Ecuador's government presenting the swift, uncontested transfer as evidence of a functioning bilateral legal process.

sideB.label: Defense-Adjacent Skepticism
sideB.text: Some legal observers note that given the near-certainty of extradition, given prior legal groundwork — an April 2025 Brooklyn indictment predating his recapture — and Ecuador's diminished capacity to hold him securely after his 2024 escape, framing the outcome as a free 'agreement' understates the practical inevitability he faced.

resolution: Macías was extradited July 20, 2025 and pleaded not guilty at his US arraignment, formally contesting the criminal charges even as the extradition itself proceeded without a formal legal challenge in Ecuador.

question: Did a Covert US Program Carry Out Drone Strikes on Ecuadorian Fishing Boats?

sideA.label: Investigative Reporting
sideA.text: The New York Times and Washington Post, citing survivor testimony, aircraft registration records tied to a Virginia shell company, and an anonymous source, reported the March 2026 strikes on the Negra Francisca Duarte II and Don Maca — and the January 2026 disappearance of the Fiorella with 8 crew — bore the hallmarks of a covert CIA action requiring presidential authorization, including a drone linked to US defense contractor Shield AI detected near one burning vessel.

sideB.label: US Government Denial
sideB.text: The US Coast Guard and Pentagon have denied any involvement, and a CIA spokesperson told CNN the agency had 'no guidance to offer' on the reporting.

resolution: Unresolved as of August 2026: no US agency has acknowledged involvement, no formal Ecuadorian government finding has been issued, and the identity of the armed men who detained survivors and handed them to the Salvadoran Navy remains officially unconfirmed.

question: Was Prosecutor Alexandra Bravo's Assassination Retaliation for Organized-Crime Work or Her Drone-Strike Investigation?

sideA.label: Fiscalía General Position
sideA.text: Ecuador's Prosecutor General's Office attributed the June 14, 2026 killing to retaliation for Bravo Cedeño's organized-crime casework in Manabí, specifically citing her June 6, 2026 investigation into the burning of 27 vessels in Manta, and noted she is the third Manta-linked prosecutor assassinated since 2022.

sideB.label: Alternative/Independent Reporting
sideB.text: Reporting from Resumen Latinoamericano and the World Socialist Web Site, published weeks after the killing, argued Bravo Cedeño's assassination should be understood in light of a separate investigation she had opened into alleged US drone strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats — a case she told Human Rights Watch in May 2026 she lacked the authority or means to investigate at sea — noting that none of the mainstream outlets covering the later CIA revelations connected her name to the story.

resolution: Unresolved: Ecuadorian authorities have not officially linked the assassination to the drone-strike investigation, and the claim rests on Tier 4 alternative-media reporting rather than confirmed findings.
